title: Gardner Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Gardner wells have a 60 ft median depth, 10 gpm median reported yield, and typical finished costs of $9,900-$18,000.
h1: Gardner, Colorado Well Information for Buyers and Builders
intro_html:
If you are looking at land or a home near Gardner, the local well records point to relatively shallow wells overall, but the range is wide. The median reported depth is 60 feet, while the deepest record reaches 775 feet. Reported yields also vary, and most permits identify an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer rather than a consistent named water-bearing formation.

This page covers permitted wells within 5 miles of Gardner in Huerfano County. The records are useful for planning, but they are not a guarantee for a particular lot. A driller still needs to evaluate the exact ground, access, casing and grout requirements, pump system, and the well permits that apply to the property.

sections.heading: Gardner well depths range from shallow to very deep
sections.html:
Among the 143 constructed wells that report a total depth, the median is 60 feet. The middle half falls between 40 and 100 feet, and 73% are under 100 feet. That gives a buyer a reasonable starting point for a shallow-well estimate, but it should not be treated as a local guarantee.

The spread matters when comparing drilling bids. Another 16% of wells are between 100 and 300 feet, while 9% fall between 300 and 600 feet. The 90th percentile is 294 feet, and one record reaches 775 feet. Permits mostly identify fractured bedrock or an unnamed aquifer, so granite and gneiss conditions can change quickly from one parcel to the next.

sections.heading: Reported Gardner well yields are usually usable, not uniform
sections.html:
Only 19 wells in the records report a pump yield, so the yield statistics are a smaller sample than the depth data. Within that group, the median reported yield is 10.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 1.9 and 13.0 gallons per minute.

The distribution gives a better sense of risk than the median alone. 5% report less than 1 gallon per minute, and 26% fall between 1 and 5 gallons per minute. Nearly half, 47%, are between 5 and 15 gallons per minute, while 21% report more than 15 gallons per minute. A low-yield well may still work with storage, but the pump test and proposed household use should be reviewed before closing.

sections.heading: The Gardner water-level records are limited
sections.html:
Only 7 permits report a static water level, so there is not enough local information to establish a dependable long-term trend. The reported median depth to water is 20 feet, and the middle half ranges from 12 to 34 feet. Those measurements describe conditions when the wells were recorded, not a guaranteed water level for a new well.

The permit history also does not show a simple decade-by-decade water-table conclusion. Records were issued from the 1950s through the 2020s, with the newest permit year listed as 2025, but permit counts are not water-level measurements. Ask for the well construction report, static level, pumping test, and any recent service history for the specific property. Neighboring wells can provide useful context, especially in fractured bedrock where conditions may change over a short distance.

sections.heading: Who has drilled around Gardner, and when
sections.html:
The local permit history reaches back to the 1950s and includes 264 wells in the Colorado DWR records. Of those, 143 are recorded as constructed. Permit activity was highest in the 2000s, with 58 permits, followed by 36 in the 2010s and 16 in the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2025.

The most frequently listed drillers are Timber Line Drilling (Pfaffenhauser, Robert G.) with 19 records, Nequette Drilling (Nequette, David J.) with 11, and Alpine Drilling & Pump Co. (Tillerson, Milton F.) with 8. These names show who appears in the records, not who is available or best for your project. Confirm current licensing, insurance, scheduling, and the scope of the bid directly with any driller.

sections.heading: What a new Gardner well may cost
sections.html:
For Gardner’s fractured mountain bedrock, the drilling model uses a rate of $65-$100 per foot. At the local median depth of 60 feet, that puts the drilled hole at about $3,900-$6,000. This is only the drilling portion and should not be confused with the total project cost.

A finished system with a pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical work is modeled at about $9,900-$18,000 at that median depth. A deeper hole, difficult access, extra casing or grout, low-yield storage, or longer utility trench can move the final bid higher. Since the local records include wells down to 775 feet, request a written estimate that separates drilling, casing, grout, pump equipment, electrical, trenching, testing, and permit-related work.

sections.heading: Gardner risks to check before closing or building
sections.html:
Fractured-bedrock wells can be unpredictable. A nearby shallow well does not prove that a new hole will find the same water, and a good reported yield does not eliminate the need for a current pump test. The local records show 5% of reported yields under 1 gallon per minute, so ask how a low-yield result would be handled with storage or a deeper attempt.

Environmental screening also matters. Within about 10 miles are 2 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 7 historic mine features. There are 0 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites in the mapped information, but that does not replace a property-specific water test. Review septic setbacks, drainfield room, access for drilling equipment, electrical service, and the well’s casing and grout records before finalizing a building plan.

sections.heading: A practical Gardner lot-buying checklist
sections.html:
Start by pulling the DWR permit and construction report for the well on the property, then compare it with nearby records in Gardner, Rye, Colorado City, La Veta, Beulah Valley, Walsenburg, or Silver Cliff. The local data show a median depth of 60 feet, but the broad range means the neighboring well that matters most is the one in similar ground and at a similar elevation.

Before buying, verify the well permit, legal use, pump test, static water level, water quality, septic approval, and the location of buried utilities. Domestic and household use appears on 76% of permits, while stock use appears on 39%; those categories do not automatically establish the rights needed for every future use. If you plan a new home, have a driller and septic designer review access, siting, storage needs, and the proposed building envelope before you commit to the lot.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Gardner, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth near Gardner is 60 feet, and the middle half runs from 40 to 100 feet. Most, 73%, are under 100 feet. The range is still wide: the 90th percentile is 294 feet, and the deepest record is 775 feet. Fractured-bedrock conditions make the exact depth parcel-specific.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Gardner, Colorado?
faq.a: The local drilling model uses $65-$100 per foot in fractured mountain bedrock. At the 60-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $3,900-$6,000. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $9,900-$18,000. Deeper drilling and difficult access can change the bid.

faq.q: How much water do Gardner wells produce?
faq.a: Only 19 local records report a pump yield. Their median is 10.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half from 1.9 to 13.0 gallons per minute. Five percent report under 1 gallon per minute, while 26% report 1-5 gallons per minute. Request a pump test for the specific well.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Gardner, Colorado?
faq.a: The permit records do not establish that every Gardner well is safe to drink. Test the property’s water before relying on it, especially because the mapped area includes 2 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 7 historic mine features within about 10 miles. Review well construction and septic conditions as part of the evaluation.

faq.q: Are Gardner wells running dry or getting deeper?
faq.a: The available records do not prove a falling water table. Only 7 wells report static water levels, with a median depth to water of 20 feet and a middle half from 12 to 34 feet. Yield data are also limited to 19 wells. Use the specific well’s recent pump test and nearby construction reports rather than assuming a regional trend.
